task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: how to measure H2-H1 change in opponent performance
statistical approaches for assessing team trait reliability (e.g., test-retest, ICC)
potential confounders in defensive performance analysis
sample size considerations for team-level trait reliability

historical_evidence.finding: Connector quality Q_p (teammate-initiated on-off PPP gap) was hypothesized to be a stable player-season attribute. Observed result: Pearson r(Q_a,Q_b)=+0.215 p=0.0297; Spearman rho=+0.242. Spearman-Brown Q~0.355, S~0.278. Sign agreement 65.7% (67/102) binomial p=0.000996. ICC(player-season)=0.216 (78.4% within). Split-half r=0.215 / SB 0.355 is too low to treat Q_p as a stable scoutable trait; most variance is within-player half-to-half.

When a defense drops a play type >=0.25 PPP H1 to H2, playsheet counter ranking predicts which alternative scored better in H2 (BEST > SECOND > AVOID). Spearman rho=-0.0639, p=0.099717, n=665 (no clear full-rank signal). Kruskal-Wallis H=32.9723, p=2.7e-05. Mann-Whitney BEST 1.257 (n=56) vs AVOID 1.092 (n=160), U=5546.0, p=0.004018.

Opponent PPP rises on the next 1-3 possessions after a star's 2nd personal foul in Q1/Q2. Including FT: lag-1 ATT=+0.204 CI[+0.163,+0.245] (artifact: FT share 41.8% vs 9.9%). Excluding FT: lag-1 +0.0486 [-0.0060,+0.0991] perm p=0.0655; lag-2 -0.0192; lag-3 -0.0272. No lag clears CI+perm+placebo. Raw lag-1 +0.204 (p=0.0005) was 41.8% FT vs 9.9% control. Apples-to-apples +0.049, not significant.

PCI (halfcourt PPP + second-chance - TO - transition leakage) explains Net Rating beyond ORtg, Pace, and FGA/poss. A R2=0.763 OOS 0.761; C R2=0.902 OOS 0.919; dR2=+0.139. Offensive-control components add +0.005 R2 beyond ORtg. Net~ORtg+leakage R2=0.948. corr(leakage, DRtg)=+0.894. PCI univariate r=+0.863 vs ORtg +0.866. Headline PCI gain is leakage tracking DRtg (+0.89); offensive-control dR2=+0.005. Baseline omitted defense by construction (Net=ORtg-DRtg).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Assessing connector quality Q_p as a stable player-season attribute using split-half reliability (Pearson r, Spearman-Brown, ICC).
failed_approaches.why: A_unanswerable (question not answerable with the data or design), [prior work], RISK:MEASURE_RELIABILITY; split-half r=0.215 / SB 0.355 was too low, most variance was within-player half-to-half.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Validating playsheet counter rankings for H1 to H2 defensive adjustments.
failed_approaches.why: E_unclear (mechanism unclear from [prior work]), [prior work], [prior work], [prior work], RISK:DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY, RISK:LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, RISK:MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RISK:SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER; full-rank Spearman was not significant.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Measuring the effect of a star's foul trouble on opponent PPP on subsequent possessions.
failed_approaches.why: C_artifact (apparent effect produced by a construction, selection or labelling flaw), [prior work], RISK:BASE_RATE, RISK:CONFOUNDING, RISK:MECHANICAL_FLOOR; the apparent effect was due to an artifact of free-throw share.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Demonstrating incremental R2 of Possession Control Index over ORtg in explaining Net Rating.
failed_approaches.why: C_artifact (apparent effect produced by a construction, selection or labelling flaw), [prior work], RISK:LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, RISK:MECHANICAL_FLOOR; the gain was an artifact of leakage tracking DRtg.

evidence_establishes: Split-half reliability for player-season attributes (e.g., 'connector quality' based on on-off PPP gap) can be very low (ICC ~0.2), with most variance occurring within the player's halves, making them untestable as stable traits ([prior work][prior work]).
Measuring defensive impacts and H2 adjustments is prone to low measurement reliability, small sample sizes, and inconclusiveness ([prior work][prior work]).
Apparent effects in basketball analytics can be artifacts of mechanical constructions, confounding variables, or leakage (FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: The specific reliability of 'a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change' as a team trait.
Whether specific methodologies or controls could overcome the inherent variability and measurement challenges to establish such a trait.
The exact magnitude of H2-H1 change attributable to defense or offense.
own_inferences: The 'defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change' is likely to be a highly noisy and variable measure, as it depends on opponent adjustments, game flow, score effects, coaching decisions, and individual player performance within a half.

Given the low reliability observed for a player-season attribute ([prior work][prior work]), it is highly probable that a more complex, game-context-dependent 'team trait' based on H2-H1 change would also exhibit very low reliability, making it difficult to establish as a stable and scoutable trait.

The available 120 team-seasons, while seemingly substantial, may be insufficient to detect a reliable signal if the underlying measurement reliability is as low as suggested by similar historical studies.
uncertainties: The exact definition of 'defense's effect' and 'H2-H1 change' for opponent performance is not specified, which could impact measurement reliability.
The specific methodology for isolating the 'defense's effect' from other game factors (e.g., offensive adjustments, game state, substitutions) is not detailed.
The optimal statistical approach for quantifying and testing the reliability of this specific team trait is not specified.

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence, particularly [prior work][prior work], strongly suggests that measures based on split-half performance, even for individual players, exhibit very low reliability, with most variance being within-player (or in this case, within-team, game-to-game). This makes it highly unlikely that 'a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change' would be a 'reliable team trait'. The other studies reinforce the general difficulty in robustly measuring and attributing defensive effects due to confounding, leakage, and low measurement reliability. This evidence changed the decision from potentially proceeding to not proceeding, as the core premise of 'reliability' is directly challenged by prior findings on similar metrics.

blocking_constraints.text: Historical evidence ([prior work][prior work]) shows that similar split-half measures for player traits have extremely low reliability (ICC=0.216), with most variance being within-player. A team trait based on H2-H1 changes is likely to suffer from the same fundamental issue, making it difficult to detect a stable signal amidst game-to-game and within-game noise.

Given the likely low measurement reliability, the available 120 team-seasons may be insufficient to achieve useful statistical power to detect a reliable team trait, if one exists, as suggested by [prior work][prior work] which noted small sample size for 665 observations.

Isolating 'a defense's effect' on H2-H1 change is complex. Opponent offensive adjustments, game state (score differential, foul trouble), substitution patterns, and coaching decisions between halves are significant confounders that could influence H2 performance independently of a stable defensive trait, as highlighted by general risks in FAM:[prior work] and [prior work][prior work].

prior_work.summary: [prior work][prior work] directly addressed the split-half reliability of a player-season attribute (connector quality Q_p, an on-off PPP gap), finding it to be untestable as a stable trait due to very low reliability (ICC=0.216) and high within-player variance. This provides strong indirect evidence that a 'defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change' as a 'reliable team trait' would also be untestable. Other studies ([prior work][prior work], FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work]) highlight general challenges in measuring defensive impacts and H2 changes due to low reliability, small samples, confounding, and mechanical artifacts.

risks.text: The core concept of 'reliable team trait' is directly threatened by the likely low measurement reliability of 'H2-H1 change' in opponent performance, as evidenced by similar split-half measures ([prior work][prior work]).

Many factors other than a stable defensive trait can influence H2-H1 changes, including opponent offensive adjustments, score effects, substitution patterns, and coaching changes. These confounders make it difficult to isolate the defense's specific and stable effect.

If the underlying signal of a 'reliable team trait' is weak and noisy, 120 team-seasons may be insufficient to achieve adequate statistical power to establish reliability, especially given the expected low measurement reliability.
The 'H2-H1 change' is a derived label from game outcomes, which can be influenced by many factors. Ensuring this measure truly reflects a stable defensive 'effect' is challenging.

Team strategies, player rosters, and league-wide trends can change over the four seasons of data, potentially affecting the consistency and reliability of any observed 'trait' over time ([prior work][prior work]).

design.estimand: The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) of a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change in points per possession (PPP) across multiple games within the same team-season, and across different team-seasons for the same team.
design.unit: Team-season for assessing across-season reliability; Game for assessing within-season reliability. The base unit for 'H2-H1 change' will be a single game's H2 PPP minus H1 PPP for the opponent.
design.sample: All 120 available team-seasons (NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26). For each team-season, include all regular season and playoff games. Exclude games with significant garbage time in either half (e.g., score differential > 20 points in the last 5 minutes of a half).
design.power: Not estimable with confidence due to predicted low reliability. A minimum of 0.8 power for detecting an ICC of 0.5 would likely require a significantly larger sample of team-seasons or games per team-season than available.
design.controls: To isolate 'defense's effect' on H2-H1 change, a robust counterfactual model would be needed. This would involve controlling for: opponent offensive strength (e.g., H1 ORtg, season average ORtg), game state (e.g., score differential at halftime, pace), player availability (injuries, foul trouble), substitution patterns, and coaching changes. A simpler approach would be to measure raw H2-H1 opponent PPP change and calculate its reliability, acknowledging it conflates defensive and offensive factors.
design.falsification: A null hypothesis of ICC <= 0.2 (based on [prior work][prior work]) for the H2-H1 change measure, suggesting the trait is not reliable. If the calculated ICC is significantly greater than 0.2 with sufficient power, the trait might be considered reliable.
design.multiplicity: Not applicable if focusing solely on the reliability of one specific metric.
design.decision_rule: The research question would be deemed 'supported' if the ICC for the defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is statistically significantly (p < 0.05) above a predefined threshold for 'reliable' (e.g., ICC > 0.5), with sufficient power. Otherwise, it would be 'rejected' (if adequately powered) or 'untestable' (if reliability is too low, as anticipated).
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular season and playoffs, as of 2026-10-06.
